You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:

CREATE TABLE museum (
    Museum_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Num_of_Staff INT,
    Open_Year TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Museum_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE visitor (
    ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Level_of_membership INT,
    Age INT,
    UNIQUE (ID)
);

CREATE TABLE visit (
    Museum_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    visitor_ID TEXT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Num_of_Ticket INT,
    Total_spent REAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Museum_ID, visitor_ID),
    UNIQUE (Museum_ID, visitor_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (visitor_ID) REFERENCES visitor(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Museum_ID) REFERENCES museum(Museum_ID)
);

When you have a final SQL query to present, always wrap it in a sql markdown code fence like this:

```sql
SELECT ...
```

This makes it easy to identify your answer. Only use one ```sql fence for your final query.

Do you mean the "rich" visitor by highest total spending across all visits, by the single largest visit payment, or do you want a top-N list? Below are example queries for each case — pick which one you want or tell me which definition/threshold to use and I can tailor it.

```sql
-- 1) Visitor with highest total spent across all visits
SELECT v.ID, v.Name, v.Level_of_membership, v.Age, SUM(vis.Total_spent) AS Total_spent
FROM visitor v
JOIN visit vis ON v.ID = vis.visitor_ID
GROUP BY v.ID, v.Name, v.Level_of_membership, v.Age
ORDER BY Total_spent DESC
LIMIT 1;

-- 2) Visitor with the single largest (single-row) Total_spent value in visit
SELECT v.ID, v.Name, v.Level_of_membership, v.Age, vis.Museum_ID, vis.Num_of_Ticket, vis.Total_spent
FROM visitor v
JOIN visit vis ON v.ID = vis.visitor_ID
ORDER BY vis.Total_spent DESC
LIMIT 1;

-- 3) Top 10 visitors by total spending (change LIMIT to desired N)
SELECT v.ID, v.Name, v.Level_of_membership, v.Age, SUM(vis.Total_spent) AS Total_spent
FROM visitor v
JOIN visit vis ON v.ID = vis.visitor_ID
GROUP BY v.ID, v.Name, v.Level_of_membership, v.Age
ORDER BY Total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10;
```
want details on visitor who bought the most tickets in one go

To return the visitor(s) who bought the most tickets in a single visit (includes ties), use:

```sql
SELECT v.ID,
       v.Name,
       v.Level_of_membership,
       v.Age,
       vis.Museum_ID,
       m.Name AS Museum_Name,
       vis.Num_of_Ticket,
       vis.Total_spent
FROM visit vis
JOIN visitor v ON vis.visitor_ID = v.ID
LEFT JOIN museum m ON vis.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE vis.Num_of_Ticket = (SELECT MAX(Num_of_Ticket) FROM visit);
```
need to get the visitor's name too

Here's a query that includes the visitor's name:

```sql
SELECT v.ID AS Visitor_ID,
       v.Name AS Visitor_Name,
       v.Level_of_membership,
       v.Age,
       vis.Museum_ID,
       m.Name AS Museum_Name,
       vis.Num_of_Ticket,
       vis.Total_spent
FROM visit vis
JOIN visitor v ON vis.visitor_ID = v.ID
LEFT JOIN museum m ON vis.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE vis.Num_of_Ticket = (SELECT MAX(Num_of_Ticket) FROM visit);
```
Also, need to make sure the ticket purchase was all in one transaction.

Good — two possibilities depending on your data model:

- If each row in visit already represents a single purchase transaction, the previous query already guarantees "one transaction". Use this to return visitor name (includes ties):

```sql
-- Case A: each visit row IS a single transaction
SELECT v.ID AS Visitor_ID,
       v.Name AS Visitor_Name,
       v.Level_of_membership,
       v.Age,
       vis.Museum_ID,
       m.Name AS Museum_Name,
       vis.Num_of_Ticket,
       vis.Total_spent
FROM visit vis
JOIN visitor v ON vis.visitor_ID = v.ID
LEFT JOIN museum m ON vis.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE vis.Num_of_Ticket = (SELECT MAX(Num_of_Ticket) FROM visit);

-- Case B: if a "transaction" can span multiple rows and you have (or add) a transaction_id column,
-- aggregate rows by transaction and then pick transactions with the largest ticket counts (includes ties).
SELECT v.ID AS Visitor_ID,
       v.Name AS Visitor_Name,
       v.Level_of_membership,
       v.Age,
       t.Museum_ID,
       m.Name AS Museum_Name,
       t.transaction_id,
       t.Tickets_In_Transaction,
       t.Total_spent
FROM (
    SELECT transaction_id,
           Museum_ID,
           visitor_ID,
           SUM(Num_of_Ticket) AS Tickets_In_Transaction,
           SUM(Total_spent) AS Total_spent
    FROM visit
    GROUP BY transaction_id, Museum_ID, visitor_ID
) t
JOIN visitor v ON t.visitor_ID = v.ID
LEFT JOIN museum m ON t.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE t.Tickets_In_Transaction = (
    SELECT MAX(Tickets_In_Transaction)
    FROM (
        SELECT transaction_id, SUM(Num_of_Ticket) AS Tickets_In_Transaction
        FROM visit
        GROUP BY transaction_id
    ) sub
);
```

If you do not currently have a transaction_id or purchase timestamp, and you need to be certain purchases are single transactions, I recommend adding a transaction_id (and optionally purchase_time) to the visit table (or creating a separate transactions table). Tell me which option matches your schema and I can adapt the query further.
Also, I need the visitor's age along with their name.

If each row in visit already represents a single purchase transaction, this query returns the visitor's ID, name and age (and museum info) for the visit(s) with the largest Num_of_Ticket (includes ties):

```sql
SELECT v.ID AS Visitor_ID,
       v.Name AS Visitor_Name,
       v.Age,
       v.Level_of_membership,
       vis.Museum_ID,
       m.Name AS Museum_Name,
       vis.Num_of_Ticket,
       vis.Total_spent
FROM visit vis
JOIN visitor v ON vis.visitor_ID = v.ID
LEFT JOIN museum m ON vis.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE vis.Num_of_Ticket = (SELECT MAX(Num_of_Ticket) FROM visit);
```

If a single transaction can span multiple visit rows, do you have a transaction_id (or purchase_time) column we can use to group rows into one transaction? If so, tell me the column name and I'll provide the aggregated query.
